newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac warns on EMU failure, France must be ready.
newsitem.headline: Chirac warns on EMU failure, France must be ready.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, warning of "very serious consequences" if Europe abandoned its planned single currency, said on Monday the project must start on time in 1999 and France must be ready to join.

In his first interview since his centre-right government was defeated in a June 1 parliamentary election, Chirac said French deficits were about half a percentage point above the three percent of output required for monetary union.
But the goal could be reached provided spending was held.
"Yes we must respect the date and conditions. That would be in France's interest," Chirac said in the traditional Bastille Day television interview.
"It would have very serious conquences for France not to do it -- very, very serious -- we would isolate ourselves," he said.
Maastricht treaty rules for the currency, due to be launched in January 1999, call for deficits to be cut to or towards three percent of gross domestic product in a lasting way.

For 1997, the reference year for deciding who joins, France's deficit is running higher, Chirac said, confirming warnings contained in a leaked handover note by conservative premier Alain Juppe, defeated at the polls on June 1.
"We have reached a current situation which must be about 3.5 percent," Chirac said.
Forced since then to share power with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, he said it was his own role as president to ensure international treaties were upheld.
But he refused to be drawn into fierce debate in France and especially Germany over whether the three-percent deficit rule should be implemented right down to the last decimal point.
"That is a subject which must be handled among Europeans and certainly not in public," Chirac said.

The new Socialist-led government has insisted this target can be interpreted as a trend rather than in precise digits, allowing France to join the single currency on time while avoiding unacceptable austerity.
It has ordered an audit of public finances to be published on July 21 after which it will set out its deficit plans.
Germany wants a strict reading of 3.0 percent as the maximum deficit level and also disagrees with Paris about how far politicians can influence the exchange rate of the new euro.

In a sign Chirac may be ready to break the French taboo which prevents a president straying beyond foreign affairs and defence, Chirac said he would remain vigilant on spending as well as other matters of key interest such as privatisation.
He said the left-wing cabinet's plans to spend money frozen by the previous administration should be matched by savings to avoid slipping off course for European monetary union.
"What I say is that 10 billion francs should be found elsewhere if we want to be among those European nations capable of taking on the single currency," Chirac said.
The government says it is planning to carry out election pledges including the promotion of public-sector jobs for young people but vows this will not involve any additional funds.

Ministers said last week they would scrap or reallocate 11 billion francs ($1.9 billion) in spending planned by the previous cabinet and spend 11.1 billion on the new measures. ($ = 6.003 French Francs)
